answer.rationale: Finance mandates 18% spend cut; incumbent has refused to reopen price this cycle (memory_c6 multi-year pricing is already locked in and memory_c4 renegotiation avenue is exhausted for this period). The primary contract expires in 14 days with no auto-renew, so inaction equals forced renewal at incumbent terms. The low-cost vendor's quote alone meets the mandate. Memory_c2 (the one I choose to verify) records that a prior switch to this same low-cost vendor cut unit cost sharply, onboarding was quick, and invoicing stayed accurate—directly relevant to delivery-risk assessment given the assembly line is at 94% with no buffer. I select memory_c2 over memory_c1 or memory_c3 because the central unknown is whether the low-cost vendor can perform reliably on a tight 14-day transition, not whether the incumbent is stable (already known) or whether dual-sourcing helps (no capacity for a second decision this cycle). I flag downstream-value risk: at 94% utilization with no buffer, any onboarding slippage hits committed volume, so the switch must include a contractual delivery-guarantee clause and a 30-day overlap/handover window before the incumbent contract lapses. I deliberately do not defer (memory_c5 pattern) because the expiry is hard and the mandate is binding; deferral would forfeit the only compliant path. I also do not add a second source this cycle (memory_c3) because capacity is limited to one decision and the quote already meets the target alone; dual-sourcing can be revisited next review. Uncertainty is preserved: the archived source record for memory_c2 must confirm the low-cost vendor's onboarding speed and invoicing accuracy before I commit; if the archive reveals caveats (e.g., quality holds, late deliveries, scope gaps) the decision reverts to a short-term month-to-month extension with the incumbent while the next review cycle addresses dual-sourcing.
